div.head: GARDEN PARTY AT WALTON LEA.
div.p: GARDEN PARTY AT WALTON LEA.

The weather on Saturday was beautiful, and the six hundred or en of people who accepted the gener- ous invitation of Alderman John Crosfleld,.l.P.. to attend a Garden Party at Walton Lea, near War- rington. secured ample means of enjoyment. Invita- tions hail been issued to the day school teachers of the town, to the members of the School Attend- ance Committee, and to the clergy and ministers of the town, and the fact of as large a number of people accepting the invitation is evidence of the way in which the action of Mr. Cro4ield in than throwing open his grounds is appreciated. At present the gardens are looking at their best, and as folk were free to wander at their own sweet will through grounds, gardens, and conservatories it is scarcely necessary to nay that it was an easy thing to pass the time both pleasantly and profit- ably. In addition to these attractions, in themselves very tempting, Mr. It. 11. Pearson's band discoursed music, and dancing took place on one of the lawns. The band of the Runcorn Seamen's Orphanage, which attracted some attention when marching through the streets of Warrington on the way to Walton Lea,also played selections, and in addition the members of the band sang several hymns. During the course of the afternoon a very appetising, as well as substant itil.tea was served in a large tent, and lawn . tennis 11/1.1 cricket were played by those who eared to indulge in those summer games. Mr. John Dewhumt sang "Sly old friend John " in very good style, and an Italian gentleman, who accom- Ponied Mr. Crosfield to England after the alderman's tour in Italy. sang the Amalfi boat song. div.head: MR. GLADSTONE.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE.

At the annual meeting of the Midlothian Liberal Association, held in Edinburgh on Wednesday, a letter was read from Mr. Gladstone expressing satisfaction that a large proportion of the work of the present xedon WOUld probably be Scotch work, though the aggregate would be very small. Notwithstanding the • ••urtaihnent of the liberty of independent membele of the oleo br purp•ses of free discnssi• In, the country would , Inse to wait for the satisfaction of its wants two : noire years, as a eonsequenee of its mistake in the ; election of 1886, in returning a majority which had Ibrilten all the promises made. The course taken by the e•-ealled Cninnist party had had the result of stimulat- ing a sentiment of nationality in Scotland and in Wake. Arrangements have been completed for the reception of • Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone at thr National Liberal Club in celebration. of their golden wedding. The event will • take place m the clubhouse on th•• 26th of July. It has • been estimated that 2,508 persons may be eon- ' veniently entertained, and tickets, price a guinea each, will be issued lid that number.

div.p: THE BETROTHAL OF PRINCESS LOUISE OF WALES.

The Queen on Thursday afternoon, formally gave her coiDent to the betrothal of Princess Louise, the eldest , daughter of the Prince and Prineess of Wales, to the Earl of Fife. The Princess was twentv-two years of age last February, and the Earl of Fife was thirty-nine not November. His lordship succeeded to the title in 1879. div.head: WIFE MURDER IN DARTFORD.
div.p: WIFE MURDER IN DARTFORD.

Richard Townwmd munlered his wife in I lgh-t., Dartford, on Thursday night. Townsend. who is nearly. 14, venty. has been living apart from his wife furs considerable time, and daring that period has ; molested and even assaulted her in the public streets. She secured a conviction against him about xi: months ago. About a quarter past nine on Thursday night he met her in ugh-st., seized her and with a sharp knife cut her throat from side to ,dc. The few people who were by secured him and held him until the police arrived. The IMMO was conveyed to the workhouse infirmary, but soon expired.

NoTICE CORRF-SPONDENTS. • 1 • ia a very ~..“•1 adv....hoe/anat. it Can

limitation of the hours of labour, or the metric- tion of output. In the House of Commons, in Tuesday, Mr. CENNISOIRME GRAHAM moved the adjournment of the House by way of protest against this restriction, mid an interesting debate ensued. His motion was seconded by a Conserva- tive member, Mr. BAMIANN, Who put the case against the Government with clearness and force.. He said:—

The Government might have declined to gend representatives to the Labour Conference, which , would have been logical, but to send represent.- tires and to forbid them to take on in the discus- ! on he hours of labour meant either that the ' labour question WOO too peril., II topic for our representatives to handle, winch was to treat our artisans like babies, or it meant that the question was so futile and absurd that, although it wait all very well for foreigners to uhiruooait, our sie,erior British wisdom declined evon to argue it. •

, Replying on behalf of the G,wernment, Sir JAMES! FNIMUNSON said her Majesty's Ministers were not prepared to buy pipularity at the price of trifling : with principles which they considered essential. This is a piece I if downright old-fashionml Toryism, ' and it is mute refreshing to come across it, how- . ever much we may disagree with it. But it witift - do in thew days, as Tories like Mr. BAUMANN ' sufficiently recognise. Granted that Parliament is not prepared either to enforce the eight-hours programme, or to pass laws restricting outrint, there could be no harm surely in a British dele- gate giving his reasons for such faith as there was in him. Arguments which are solid in Great Britain will be equally solid whey advanced in Switzerland. Besides, if we are right, and the Conference is disposed to go wrong, considerations of courtesy and Inimmity would suggest that , we should try to keep others in the right pith. IBut the Government have not even been consist- ! rot in their restriction, for they will permit of the British representative taking part in proposals for restricting Sunday labour. There is something wrong about a principle of non-interference which is to apply six days in the week and break down on Sunday. The f.t of the matter is the qui.- : ties as to how far Parliament shoold regulate adult labour is Ante which is certainly open to dis- cussion ; and, if we are list much mistaken, it will, before many years are ovar, he discussed during election campaigns and in the House of Commons. There is a growing feeling in favour of the move- lutist for working eight hours per day only ; and it is mit to be pooh-poohed and dismissed as some- thing altogether visionary. In Victoria, as Mr. I GRAITAM reminded the HOUSO, the working-men of the colony have recently met to celebrate the twenty-fourth annivemary of the inauguration a the eight-hours system : and what agitation has accrunplished in Australia, agitation may Remus- plink in England. In several of the States id the American Union, tint, laws have been passed for the regulation of adult male labour. Hitherto legislation in this country has been confined tin regulating the labour of women and children ; lint it is preposterous to say that any proposed extension of the principlo shall not even he di. cussed at an Internathmal Conference. It seems to us that such a Conference is precisely the place where it should be discussed—in the first install.. A proposal to restrict labour to eight hours per day would afford a British' delegate a splendid opportunity of pointing to the excessively long hours worked on the Continent 1121 compared with the hours of work in this country, and of urging that the first thing to be done was to pint other nations on a level with • England. We are strongly of opinion that there must be is successful movement in this direction on , the Continent before English artisans and labourers can hope to enforce the eight-hours system. It is consequent upon the long hours, low wages, and the technical training of our Continental neighbours that we are more and more feeling the pressure of competition. The pressure would be increased by shortening the hours of labour at home, and it might in some cases prove to he the last straw that would break the camel's back. We are a long way from getting Parliament to legislate on the subject, when even its discussion is tabooed by a Tory Government. Our own opinion is in Iw:q.t..] with that of the majority of Trades I:Monists, and that is that action should Its taken independent of appeal to Parliatnent. Efforts of this kind have suoceeded before without the help of the Legislature, and they will succeed again, if they are well-directed and on right lines.

'Truth " says :—I see that Mr.Oltrien's action against Lord Salisbury for slander mines on for hearing at the Manchester Summer Assizes next month, and that it is announced that Mr. Justice I Stephen tool Mr. Justice Grantham will he on the 'circuit then. As the latter was a very strung party Tory, mid was made a judge because of his being party Tory, by the defendant, I trust that he will himself perceive that he ought not to try this action.

Mr. O'Brien rooms to he in good fighting form. Besides the action against Lord Salishary. he has commencisi proceedings against Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., for alleged libel arising out of a letter written by the member for South Tyrone to the "Times," in which it wa.s stated that Mr. O'Brien had refused relief to a man :it Gweedore because he was a Pro- testant. Mr. O'Brien may be stripped and ren- dered helpless when in gaol, hut whilst he ix out of prison he means to strike blow for blow.

The iigitation for Home Role is growing in Wales and in Scotland or well an in Ireland. The' Daily Telegraph," which cannot he called Liberal.says i— " Looking at the question without prejudice, we are compelled to admit that the claim of Scotland too Legislature at Edinburgh is stronger than that of Ireland.- This is a large admission, and it is a sign of progress. Verily, this generation shall not pass away until we have Hone Rule all round.

The pretty actress may make a hit ofi the stage RS well as Ofl; but occadonally the hit is something of a miss. The 'POII Mall Gazette" says its representative was "informed on Monday morning, by Mr. George Lewis,that Miss Phyllis Broughton's action against Lord Dungan for breach of promise of marriage had been settled. The ter.; of settle- merit are a payment of I:2,500 to Miss Brought.. and Lord Dangan undertakes tO pay all the eels. Poor Lord Dangan ; he will be "sorry he spoke."

As the outcome of a representative conference on the housing of the poor, held at Sheffield, on Monday night, a resolution was passed appointing a Provisional Committee to consoler the question, and to decide as to the best means of bringing pressure to bear on the Corporation to put in force the Public Health and Artisans Dwelling Act It would be well if similar stops wore taken in this. part if the country. Corporations need pressure putting upon them, for it frequently happens that aldermen and. town councillors are the owners of pr.,prty which might really to be closed as unfit for human habitation.

The following is tube the programme of the SiViSS Labour Conference, which was the subject of dismission in the House of Commons on Tues- day :-1. The prohibition of Sunday labour. 2. The fixing of a minimum age for the admission of children into factories. 3. Fixing a maximum length of the day's work for young operatives. 4. Prohibition of the employment of young persona or women in works especially injurious to health or otherwise dangerous. 8. Restriction of night work for young pyrsona mid women. 6. Ile mode of carrying out conventions which may he min- chided.

Lancashire were badly beaten on Tuesday at the hands of Notti by an innings and 59 rims. The liest scores for Lancashire were made by Briggs, who put 0, 38 in his . first and Sir, his second innings, and V. Ward, who by neat cricket ran up to Sun his second innings, though I his first attempt was entirely barren. On the Notts side I their emelt batsman, Barnes, added is, his reputation by Iscoring 102.

Thecontinued inclusion of Mr. S. AL fix:afield in the Lancashire county team seems to be a son, point with some writers on cricket. This is wird the "Athletic Journal "hat now to sav On the subject:—" We give way to no one in oar aamiration of Mr. S. M. Crosfield an a sportsman, but we really think he should stand out 01 the Lancashire eleven until such time as he plays himself into form. Another week or two may see great difference in his play, and it would be an easy matter to reinstate him in the eleven."

Luck was against the Warrington Hub on Saturday.l They went to Bolton, but not to conquer. Alas ! They I were beaten, and that right well. The defeat, as it ' were, was " rubbed in;' for when Bolton had batted how men they " declared." Thy had then run on 178, and proceeded to dispose of Warrington, who were all oat for 83 runs. In justice to the local men, how- ever, it should be stated that they only took sin of the regular first tram players, and that there was some very smart individual play.

Given fine weather, the cricket match at Widnes on Thursday neat—Police v. Tmdesmen—will be a great : success. Up to the present about 2,000 tickets havo heen disposed of, and the hospital for whose benefit the game is arranged, will receive a well deserved donation. Smierintendent Johnston, the prteident ot the Police Club, has taken a deep interest in the event, and he will be delighted should his men in blue come off the con- titterers.

In connection with Runcorn Cricket Club, a lawn tennis club has been formed, and the courts are being laid nut. The club is formed ton late in the season to achieve distinction, but much pleasure may be the result at the new move, and a void will be filled. CYCLE NO.

The hot weather we have been having lately has had I rather an unfavourable effect on the greens in the neighbourhood, and as a matter of fact it has been almost too aultry to play howls at all. Some enthusiastic devotees, however, have kept it up all along, with the result that their friends pmfoss to notice that day by day they are bsotiming thinner and thinner—wasting their satiatanae, as it were, on the "green" arena of pleasure.

There was quite a migration of flomemarket-street tradmmen to the Horse and Jockey on Tuesday after- noon. They didn't go to imbibe, or even to play bowls, but to undertake the not over pleasant duty of •• sitting on a body." It happened that Coroner Brighouse was delayed at Widnes, and to fill up time a few of the jury- men began trying the green. After the Coroner had turned up, and the grave duty for which the jury had been a.qrernbled had been discharged, the aforesaid few could not resist the temptation of staying behind to have just another game, and then another. I don't know whether they made a day of itor not, but! should fanny some of them, when they got home, would have to make it out that the inquest had been a remarkably long one. •• Very sad case, my dear ; grave responsibility, tint dutim of this kind must be conscientuously discharged.

Commenting on the recent great chew to at New York, a contemporary says i—The pnronnel of the men engaged in the long struggle for intellectual swim reacy affords much of interest. Yschigorin is a hand- some fellow of about 60, with a pair of fine piercing black even; his style of play is full fir beldnest and dash, while his "book " knowledge io most extensive. Formerly an attaelul of the Russian Diplomatic Corps, he seems now decided to yield to the fascination of the game and devote himself entirely to it. flit score of 6 games against Steinitt's 10 in their recent match is the best stand there has been made against the unconquered Bohemian. In striking contrast is I'Veits—" the quiet ! little Austrian in gray "—who day by day has gone steadily on maintaining wonderfully even force of play, I seldom or never equalling the highest efforts of his strenretrivals,nr, on the other hand, falling much below , hit average. linnaborg, one of the few men who have twice carried off a first prize. alto at the board almost like a statue, and intoner more dangerens than when. with eyes lialfielosed. he appears least moved. Meleoxl is a , spare youth of 10, twice winner of the Canadian Chem- Ipionship. Impetuous and often overhasty, he still succeeded in snatching a win from Blackburn° at a i critical stage of the acore.

Bird, who is extremely popular in the North of Eng- land, was the oldest player competing, but giving place . to now in enthusiasm and freahnms oA style. His play • was, as it usually is in long °tridents, very uneven—one day winning finely against the strongest, and the next losing to the weakest. Arriving fifty minutes late on the day he had to play Lipshatz in the first meld, the lime I limit required him to make his first. fifteen 11100 PS Within I ten minutes, while his opponent, of course had his full I hour. And the veteran actually made the stipulated , numberof moves inane minute, and at the same time I secured the better game !

But tie great figure in the first round and beginning ' of the second was Illackburne,who woo in fine form, and ' was called by the American great" The tliant.'"flien Ids chess was of the highest order, and in his wins he iieeinial to tower above all, notably, in the games against nunsberg, and Lipshiitt, either of which would prove him a groat master. No one played a better gatne than he did, and his friendit have every reason to think that had he only stayed a little longer they might have hailed the winner in him.

FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR. JOHN TINSLEY.

THE DEATH OF ALDERHA:. ,PIERPOINT. Mr. John Firepoint, an Alderman of the Borough of Atiarrimiton, slhd. on Saturday morning, at his residency Tower Matte. Lodge-lane, Be %trey, at the ag.• of siatty-fone from sync ipt, of the heart. The event, which was painful in its suddenness, happened at about eleven o'cloek in toe morning. M Pierpoint had just been visited by lint medical attendant. Dr. Adams, awl was preparing tu leave the house for bis office, when hew.,, suddenly seized with illness, and died almost immediately. Though his death was altogether unexpected he 'hail not for some time been in good healun, and had recently paid a visit to Llandudno. Last alonday week Int: wend in business to Si, Helens, hut as lie dish not feel sell he returned home, and was on the billowing day unable to carry out his intend ion of going to Buxton for a further period of rest. Pierpoint, who was born in t year 1024, was the sec nisi son of Mr. William ii' rpoint --head of tine tire! of Messrs. Pierpoint and Illephent, builders, Crown-st. Ile was a native of the tow n, awl with Ii view to bet:timing an architect Inc workrel some time at the bench as a joiner, and subsequently gained experience in a Liverpool office. Rae rnirsg to Warrington he commenced practise as an architect. awl at the same time became the landlord of the Blue Bell Inn. Afterwanls be took the pre- sent business premises in Bold-st , anti went to live in Palmyra-square, but over twenty years ago he removed to his late residence at liewsey. The firm that lie ft/Muted was afterwards known as Pier- point and Hughes, then as Pit:roc:int and Son, later as Pierpoint and Adams, and finally as Pierpoint and Fraser. The late Alderman, who leaves a widow and several children, was in 1087 appointed a magistrate for the borough by tile Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. and for many years he acted as overseer. A few weeks ago he was elected tin no aldermanie chair, which he only occupied at one meeting of the Council, but he had for wine years prior to tlien been a member of the Town Council. Before the general election of MIS lie was a member of the Liberal party, and occupied a Seat ass, liberal in the Council Chamber. lie was in office for several years, antl t lieu retires! from the Corporate body. In 18141, liovrever, he again sought election, this time as a Conservative, and was returned as one of the representatives of the South- west Ward. Ile remained with the Conservative party, and retained his seat on the Council continu- ously up to the time of his death. Ho was a member of the Cemetery, Markets, General Pur- poses, and Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee, and of the latter he was deputy-chairman. His election as Alderman, in place of the late Alderman Webster, took place on the 7th, of last month. The late Mr. Pierpoint was for seven years tine chairman of the Warrington Licensed Vietuallera'Aaaociation, and an illuminated address was presented to him in recognition of Ilia services on his retirement from that office. Ile took much interest in this Aasocia- Don, but the Society the welfare of which he had most at heart was the one that is known no the "Old 31en'a Christmas Dinner and Aged Women's Tea Committee," of which he was either president or vice-president for about a quarter of a century. TIIE FUNERAL. At noon on Tuesday the remains of the late Alderman were interred at tile Cemetery, the service at the grave- . side being read by the Rev. S. Wilkinson, vicar of St. Paul's Church, where the deceased hat been a regular attendant. The funeral procession, which left Tower HOU., shottly after eleven o'clock, was joined at the Cemetery gates lw a number of members of the Corpora- tism, of the Conservative Association and Club, and several gentlemen representing the Old Meteel Annual Dinner and Aged Women's Tea Committee. The late Mr. Pierpoint had for many years formed one ; of the congregation of St. Peas Church, liewsey-st.,and the Vicar (the Rev. S. Wilkinson) preaching there on , Sunday morning, thus referrol to his death —"it: was , mly as I returned from the funeral of the late Mr. Tinsley that a friend net Inc at Market Gate and told , me that a respected member of this congregation, one I who had worshipped in this church long before I came , into the parish, who had been an officer amongst an, and , who had been most regular in his attendance here, had : been suddenly called away ; I allude to Mr. John Pierprint. I need not ask you to prey for that poor widow, who now suffers in her solitude. You will, lam sure, pray to Grit that he will support her in her hour of bereavement, because we do know this—that Hod especially promises to Ire a hustxurd to the widow and a father to the fatherk'sts. Let me ask for your prayers on behalf of her whose husband worshipped in this church not Sunday or the Sunday before, but who was yesterday morning suddenly called away. All theist things teeth you and tne that we ought to be ready, because the Master may come when we little expect Idm. Both our brother' who have been called away were strong, hale, and hearty men, and, as we thought, had many years of usefolness before them. lint Ood has called them home, and the lesson we most learn this morning is—e Be ye, therefore, ready, tor in such an hour as ye think not the Lord cornett," MAGISTERIAL REFERENCE. The Mayor of Warrington (Alderman T. II Sutton), on taking his seat at the usual sitting of the Borough Bench on Monday morning, said it was his rtainful duty to refer to the loss that they had sustained since they !last met by the death of their brother magistrate, Mr. , John Pierpoint. Mr. Pierpoint, who sat on that bench, in the performance of his duties, until about a fortnight ago, W.oa now no more. He WM very much shoeked on • I Saturday to learn during Om funeral of the late Mr. John Tinsley, of the sad lox: that thcv had sustained, which , addrsl another to the valuaido lives departed dm- int., the last year or two. The late Mr. Pier- . point had attended that Court regularly almost every Monday, and had done his duty faithfully ' and well. His well-known More not only in that Omit but throughout Warrington, would, he thought, be very ninth missed. He wished to ask the deputy-clerk to be good enough to convey to the widow and tamily of the deceased magistrate their expressiom of sympathy and condolence at the loss they had sustained. —Mr. G. F. F. White, deputy-clerk, concurred on behalf of his father I and himself with the remarks made by his worship, and ) I the business of the Court was then proceeded with.

OnT uesslav morning, at the Barley mow Hotel, Church-et., Mr. R. Dobson, deputy coroner; held an inquest into the eireumatancea of the death of Francis Buffos, 35 years of age, who had resided in Back Cooper-4. (fr. W. Shaw. missionary. was foreman of the jury. and Inspector O'Donnell was present on behalf of the police. --Thomas Jennie,ts, a seaman, identified the body an that of Ins sinter. She was a widow, but hod cohabited with a !labourer nantsl John Rowlands. On Sunday unrhe she I 11.1 a large quantity of rum and was tipsy. Of the people mllO were about forty were killed outright, most of them hong literally blown to atoms. div.head: MR. GLADSTONE AND THE CRIMES ACT.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE AND THE CRIMES ACT.

Mr. Sydney Hal Wax recently wrote to Mr. Gladstone ,etiliogills attention to the fact that at Falcarragh, rooms. Donegal, since the commencement of the year there had only been soms cronvietionA for trivial offences under the onlinary law, As against 164 committals under the Crimes Act Mr. Hallifaz asked Mr. Gladstone if in his opinion these figures did not fur- nish an answer to the ea-intention that therrimes Act had created no new crimes. To this Mr Gladstone has replied as follows i--•• My dear sir,-1 thank you for the interesting intimation, which I take for granted is from an authentic somer. I agree as to the inference touch- ing the ahsurd allegation of the Government that there on', no new crimes under the Art of 1887,—Your faithful and obedient, W. E. tliaos.rnas."

div.p: BURNL I Y G AZETTE, Februory 23rd. :UT': lot of those who toil from day to day in the bowels of the `4,10 earth is not a very agrt:eable one. Apart from the terrible •• risks of which we are so often reminded by a calamitous explosion, all its thrilling scenes, the collier,has to pursue his work at circumstances of great hardship. Mr. Moses Knowles, of in;. x kat] Road, Burnley, has luta FOLIC experience of the trying coilditions of Idiotic in sonic of the deeper coal mines of this country. He relates how he has repeatedly had to work for hours crouched in ten or twelve inches of water and the cold liquid at the same time dropping all over his body from above. Happily such conditions of employment are almost unknown in the Burnley district but Mr. Knowles has had to .ucounter them in other mining localities, and has been a painful •1. in consequence. He first I--- —1 commenced with pains in his • !. gradually extended to other parts of the bodv.• " 1 _ _ •

THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS. haven.. far refrained from taking any personal action in referenee to this unsavoury subject, but am unable any longer to keep silent. The nuisance is of such a dreadful character that I am compelled to spcak out, and in the out empkatic mainsar to enter my earnest protest against its further continuance. the I indction of such n revolting nuisance nu the inhabitants 1 is to the last degree cruel, and reflecta the greatest iis.. credit on the woalled Sanitary Committoe. I ani a tradesman in the neigloSsurhaul, and the anuovanee arising few tic o horrid stench is at timm a:linost unendurable. Since the advent of the recent hot weather. it has ben sickening and disgusting to a degree almost inc,inceivablu How long is the horrid nuisance to vontinue? It forms the stock aubject of conversation with nearly every customer who conies into my shop. . Representations have been repeatedly made to the 1 Sanitary Committee about it, but they are practically I • Ignored. lithe nuisance gots on much longer. I shall sumpnt to toy neighbeurs the dmirability resort- ing to other meastum—rif a forcible and energetic character. The Sanitary Committee are merely the servants 111 the telhhe —not the masters--nod the sooner then are made to appreciate this fat the better it will 1 le, tor them and all concerned. They certainly ought to 1 be the last people in the world to poison the atmosphere I of crowded districts with such a nauseating effluvla as is diffused by thew latest and crowning triumphs of a fastidious and scientific civilization. A corcry Conti' JUDD?. AND lIIS DEARIND. Sir,-1 happened to be present at the Warrington County Court on Thursday last, and was witness of a very remarkable incident. A ease was being heard be- fore a jury, in whieli damages were claimed for assault, and I was present when the foreman announced that the ! jury had found for the plaintiff, with damages one farthing." After the jury had been discharged it trail- ! spired that the judge had taken down the verdict as ! giving "one wln.l" damages, and he refused to be coll..; gincisl that he hail made a mistake. Even when the foreman attire jury was brought hack, and stated the ' the jury bad awarded "one farthing," his Honor n, fused to rectify the emir, which was palpably his OWII, and took refuge behind the statement that, as the Buoy had been discharged, he could not re-open the case. 'ilk may IR' good raw, but it is very queer justice. I had no interest in the case, but had I been the person whose expenditure was increased Inan a farthing ton sovereign. I should have felt very much inclined to kick, recast the risk of contempt of Court. 'foe verdict was given distinctly, and the only supposition is that the judge must be just a little deaf, as regards the canned ear that was nearest the jury box. But if the mistake sin judge, or the deafness of a judge, is allowed to override the verdict of " twelve Rood men and true," what need is there of a jury at all? Had it bettor not he the judge, the wh j ole udge, and nothing but the judge. Tradesmen would rather be looking after their businesses than spending time in a jury-box, only to find the result of their deliberations upset at the gnigh.—Youre he. Warrington, June 28th, 1686.
PROTEST.

MR. WILLIAM DIGGLE.—A SERIOUS MIS-STATEMENT. Sir,—ln your issue of Saturday last Mr. niggle makes an assertion which, if true, ',odd justify the mtepayenr of Warrington in refusing to continue their confidence in the Sanitary Committee for a single day longer. Mr. niggle says, that he propheeied sometime ago, that the pipes which convey the excreta from the depas to Longford would "silt up," and he goes on to any, " now learn that a little while ago an obstruction did take place, and in the examination of • certain bend in the pipes it was found no stopped up, that swan could only get his three 'hirers therein." When I remind your readers that these pipes are six inches in diametei inside, and that they have only been in Use for about two yea., and, further, that the ;unrest of the method of convey- ing the excreta from the intercepting depotto Longford depends absolutely upon the freedom of these pipes from either " corrosion " or " silting," it will be seen at once, how grave is the character of Mr. Diggle's assertion. Not only would such an aasert ion (if true) involve the whole of the members of (ho Sanitary Committee in a most serious liability, bur the professional repute of the Borough Surveyor would be irremediably damaged. To Mr. Longdin the failure of the scheme in quer ion would him meant professional extinction, and, therefore, before Mr niggle had rushed into print in the manner he has done, he was bound, by all that is fair and honest, to ascertain the correetniss; r otherwise,of the story to which he has, unfortunately, lent tor creduloue an ear. Permit mob) tay, at once, that Mr. niggles assertion is an absolute fabrication from beginning to end. There is not the i shadow of a shade of truth n any part of it. The pipes in question are as free in their working to-dav: as on the day they WIdA first put down and tried. Thin is proved by the fact that the delivery of the material from each of the depots takes exactly the same time to the minute Ro- an when first put into sine. Further than this, from the time they were first laid until now, the pipes have never been uncovered for ant yurpose whatsoever Con- nected with the object for %Ouch the!, were intended. The Sanitary Committee. under the able guidance of ' their respected mid worthy chairman. have enough to do to cope with the actual difficulties which are constantly facing them in their efforts to maintain and improve the health and surroundings of the people of Warrington, and I feel confident that every man who loves honesty and fair play, will condemn in no measured terms the reckless irresponsibility of such statements as Mr. niggle's, which are made without the slightest founda- tion. but like all lies. if given a moment'a start, often do infinite mischief before they are overtaken.—Yours truly. HENRY ROBERTS. 17, Museum-nt., Warrington, June 27,1889.

A motion was made on Saturday in the Chaneery I Division of the High Court of Justice, before Mr. Justice I Chitty, that the action by the attorney-General 311 the relation ,ii the Mcmey Itosks and Harbour Board against the Manchester Ship Canal Genpany should be advanced I and heard immediately. The action asks for an injunc- tion against the defendant company and it: ointractor , and others to restrain them from making certain em- bankments alleged to be out of the line of the plans and : sections winch were before the Parliamentary Com- mittee which sanctioned the scheme of the Manchester Ship Canal. As the matter is urgent, the works seeding rapidly, and as in the present ccridition ot the I cause list before the courts there is little chance of the case being heard in regular rotation before the long vacation, the motion for expediting the hearing, either by Mr. Justice Chitty taking it out of its turn or trans. On Saturday la.st, John Leach,a young man,living with his parents in Bank-at.. went out on a fishing expedition with the smack Village Boy. He mae accompanied by Thomas 000kaon,16 years of age.who had not bad any experience in Balling. On Satur- day afternoon the boat was picked up off Bastham by several men belonging to a schooner, but neither Leach nor Cookson wereon board. On Saturday, Sunday and Monday a number of boats left Widnes in search of the young fishemien but without success. The father of Leach wont out again on Tuesday, and on the sand- bank between F.astham and Oarston, he found the dead body of his son lying. Cookson's body was washed ashore at Eastliamontho same day.—Mr. w. T. flusbandoleputy coniner, held an inqnest at Mersey Hotel on Thursday afternoon on the body of Leach, which had been taken to his parent's house.—ltobert Leach, fisherman, of 22 Bank-at., deposed that the deceased was his son, and a-as 23 years of age. He corroborated the above details and said ho teas fishing himself within two miles of where his son and Cookson were drowned. Ile had his atten- tion called to the Village Boy by seine men, and he at once rerognised it as his boy's bat. TI i. nen on a schooner had told witness that they heard in noise, and, looking up from their dinners, saw both Leach and sokson in the water.—The Coroner remarked that the Ifather had no doubt the young men were accidentally drowned ; aad the jury returned a verdict acconlingly.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. F. 11. flossage and Mr. J. Brock, two Irishmen named Patrick Leonard and John Crawley, were charged with being found in an unentered excise manufactory, to wit, an illicit still, at No. I, Catherine-st., and did knowingly aid, assist, and were concerned in the manufacture of excisable , goods and commodities.—Mr. John Paterson,a super- visor of inland revenue. Liverpool, conducted the prosecution, and stated that on the previous day he !obtained &search warrant, and visited the house of ! Leonard about three o'clock in the afternoon. The first thing his eye rested upon was the jar pro- duced, which smelled strongly of illicit spirit," nail it had been recently used. Ile then descended into the cellar, and there found a still, which was standing On a brick-still seat, with a fireplace underneath, having a Ilse carried up she wall, and enclosed in new brick work. In another part of the cellar, was a fermentation tub, containing about 30 gallons of wash, or wort, in process of fermentation. Ile procured two samples and destroyed the rest. He searched for the still head and worm, but failed to find them. Mrs. Leonard mid these operations were the work of a man, who left about a week previously, and who would return on Thursday night to complete the opendion. She said his name was John (7rawley, hut aftersvanls said she could not renumber the aurname of the man. She mid he was making is tonic. Tilt...cooler," through which the spirit flowed when the still was at work, was alas found. The I prisoner Leonard mid he knew nothing about the I matter. tea loss, WiliCh was locked up, was found a letter addressed to Mr. and Mrs. Leonard, from a non named O'Hare, of 12, Cornmarket-st., Newry, Inland, and it evidently referred to illicit distillation and men- tioned Cntwley's name. The prisoner Leonanl said he , knew nothing about it, lad Mrs. Leonard said it related ' entirely to the purchase of wane cows. Ile arrested Leonard an the occupier of the hOUSP, and Crawley as a lodger. From information received la knew that Crawley had been engaged in illicit operati.ms. As they were leaving the house Mrs. Iwonanl bad Crawley to remember that the letter wanabouteows. —Joseph Vincent Pudic, and Thomas Richard Philips. revenue officers, corroborated. The latter said he found , a small areraint book in which contained item" protheen Mr. Paterson mid Leonanl kept a milk shop and dealt in general gtmls.—lnspector Keighley also gave evident-a—Nelson Bromilow, a bricklayer, said he rrtseieesi the order from Mrs. Ivennanl to bilikt the fireplace kr. in the collar, and Patrick Leonard handed him the hricks whilst he wan at work.—William John Moreland, tinsmith, Waterloo-1,3d, deposed that the can produced was repaired at his shop, and Hole tuba made for it. He did not know it was toaiiihs' be used pOO a year.--withstill like that to itefeunsi the reeensr ssf IBoth prisoners denied all knowledge of the affair, but Mr. Gossage mid the Bench considered the cane very . clear and mch prinoner ins fined £3O and costs. div.head: TERRIBLE RAILWAY
div.p: TERRIBLE RAILWAY
ACCIDENT IN PENNSYLVANIA
4 PERSONS KILLED.

New Thou, WKONENDAY.---An appalling railway accident oecurred this morning, at Latrobe, Penn- sylvania. A heavy goods train left Johnstown for Pittsburg, and a number of men who bad been employed in clearing the ruins, becoming Isick of their unsavoury work, climbed clan- ' destinely on board, in the hope of getting a free ride to their homes. II hen near Latrobe, the train suddenly left the rails, and was completely wrecked, some of the waggons being piled one on top of the other. Not until that moment was it realised how many passengers were on the train. Their agonising cries drew attention to their presence. Those who were not killed outright were pinned helplessly beneath the ruins of the waggons, and in that position met a hideous death. A , • quantity of lime, which the goods train carried, was net on fire by the water from the disabled engine, and the flame, thus strangely kindled, spread quickly to the wreckage of the waggons. Nothing could he effectually done to rescue the poor wretches, and! over forty perished.
LATEST. NEW YO., Painsr.—The number of deaths from the Railway accident in Pennsylvania ainount, to 45.

That the Conservative Club at Widnes is begin- ning to have a finished appearance and an imposing opening ceremony may shortly be expected. The company who are floating, have shown themselves adepts in the begging line. Subscriptions amount- ing to over .£l,OOO have been obtained, and this large sum will go towards increasing the value of the slitueliolders scrip, As the results of the entire expenditure belongs so the limited com- pany. A dividend is a very remote possibility, however, so that after all the shareholdta will profit little.
That perhaps it will yet become what Major Cross, the local Tory leader christened it. the Liberal Club.

That in process of time one may become callous ,to anything, but the frequency of accidents in Widnes many of which have a fatal termination, is becoming quite apalling. For several weeks past ! the record has been a fearful one. In most in- stances these accidents could be prevented by the exercise of s lilt lo care on the part of the work- men concerned, but daily contact with danger renders them inconsiderate and careless. Stringent regulations by the employers might have a whole- some effect.

That the idea of establishing a district nurse in Runcorn is a capital one, and, if curried out in a proper spirit, her services would be a great boon to the poor folks. Unfortunately sectarian feeling has been imported into the affair, and it must be said that the bazaar on Thursday had a distinctly " Church" appearance, notwithstanding that a pro- minent Wesleyan performed the opening ceremony. People cannot forget the Vicar's desire to haves num who was a churchwoman and could speak word for God ; apparently an innocent wish enough, but to Nonconformists it seemed an attempt to proselytise in the homes of those "without the pale," and they hare constquently heist aloof.

BAZAAR AND FETE AT RUNCORN. With the object of raising funds to provide a ! district nurse for Runcorn, a bazaar and open-air ' fête was commenced in • field at Higher Runcorn on Thursday afternoon. A committee, with the vicar of the parish as chairman, have hail the pro- ject in hand for some months, and the fine was arranged under the auspices of Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., Lady Brooke, Dowager Lady Brooke, Mr. J. Brooks. of Morley farm. was found to be saliorinu from the disease, and sulvequently it was, by order of the lo.ral authority, destroyed. o

SAL%Cooonnoa- TIONAL. —This match was played at Onghtrington on Saturday, and a very pleasant game resulted in a decided victory for the home learn by 29 runs and fire wickets to spare. 9lessrs. O. F. Brazendale, J. Houk, 11. ornaron, and F. Bracendale batted well for the home : team. Mr. Blakemore, a member of the Oughtrington eleven, whilst hitting, got rather seriously hurt, and has I bet. incapae.Bitted Irons his duties since the accident.

Lvmnt Court, on Tuesday, three men, named Patrick 'Joyce, John Philbin, and James Lee, described as hawkers, were brought up before Mr. G. B. D•whorst charged with stealing a money bon and 84d.. tno property of Mr. Win. Nuttall,Dollington, on the 24th inst. It appears that about six o'clock on Monday evening the three men called at the house of Mr. MuttalL There was no one in the house at the time, the money box being on the drawers in the kitchen. The men were seen to leave the back door, and on Mrs. Nuttall returning she missed the box containing the money. She at onto', informed the police, and Sergeant I*Male, of Lvmm, apprehended the prisoners. Some time afterwards, whilst Sergeant Mcilale wali walking , along the road, he found the box broken open and the ' money miming. Mr. Dewhurst said that there was not Isufficient evidence to convict the three men, and they were accordingly discharged.

div.head: SERIOUS TRAP ACCIDENT AT GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: SERIOUS TRAP ACCIDENT AT GRAPPENHALL.

An alarming trap accident occurred at GrapPcb- ball Bridge yesterday afternoon. Mr. Cox, pork butcher, Winviick-street, Warrington, accompanied by hie wife and daughter, were returning to War- rington, and had just crossed the canal bridge when the horde shied. The trap was violently overturned and its occupants hurled into the adjoining field which is lower than the road. Mr. Cox was dis- covered to have a broken arm, and Mrs. Cot's face was seriously injured. The girl was not so badly hurt, but the trap was so damaged that the injured persons had to be conveyed home in another one.

A CHILD DROWNED AT LATCHFORD. COURAGEOUS ATTEMPTED RESCUE BY TIIE

div.head: FATHER.
div.p: FATHER.

Another drowsing fatality in the Old ()nay canal occurred on Monday evening. Some children were playing near the swing bridge no the Wilderspool side of the Black Bear bridge, when a little girl named Ilarriet Iligham, live years of age, fell into the water. The bridge, it may he mentioned, is not unprotected at the sides but the apertures between the hers are sufficiently wide to allow a child ;to fall through. After the accident an alarm was ; quickly given and the father of the child, who ; lives close by, ran to the canal and seeing his daughter, at once jumped in. Not being a swimmer his efforts to save the child were unavailing and he was him-elf very nearly drowned. His wife came to his assistance and endeavoured to pull I him out but failed, and lie was sinking for at hird time when a man named tiewge Adamson 3,lc- retqled in drawing him Silt. The littl.• girl haying tirtialty sunk to the bottom, grappling for the body was at once begun. A couple of strong swimmers and divers also volunteered their services. After the search had been continued for nearly half- an-hour P.C. Bell, who bad been called to the scene. succeeded in drawing the body to the site and it was taken to the parents' house. An inquest was lull on Tuesday evening at the Black Bear Inn, Latchford, and a venlict of accidental death was rut urned.
